# Bi-Planar Fluoroscopy System for Simultaneous Multi-View Imaging

## Field of the Invention

The present invention concerns methods and systems for bi-planar fluoroscopy utilizing dual fluoroscopes mounted to C-arms. These systems are configured to provide both lateral and anterior-posterior (AP) imaging of a patient, enabling comprehensive visualization during medical procedures.

## Overview of the System

The system employs two fluoroscopes, each independently positioned and aimed to capture a distinct viewing angle or orientation of the target anatomy. In a typical configuration, one fluoroscope is oriented to provide a lateral view while the other provides an anterior-posterior view. This dual-orientation approach allows the operator to observe the target region from two complementary perspectives concurrently, eliminating the ambiguity that can arise from reliance on a single imaging plane.

## Fixed Positioning and Control Mechanisms

A key feature of the system is the ability to maintain both fluoroscopes in fixed or locked positions throughout a procedure. Once the C-arms have been appropriately positioned and locked, the fluoroscopes can be operated remotely through proximally located control mechanisms. These mechanisms may include foot pedals or voice commands, with each control being specific to an individual fluoroscope. This design allows the operator to activate imaging from either device as needed without altering the established positioning.

The control mechanisms are specifically designed for use by a single operator. This operator may engage each fluoroscope either individually or simultaneously, depending on the imaging requirements of the moment. By consolidating control in this manner, the system streamlines the imaging workflow and reduces the need for additional personnel.

## Clinical Applications and Advantages

The system is particularly beneficial for spinal procedures, such as pedicle screw placement and kyphoplasty balloon positioning, where accurate multi-planar visualization is essential to safe and effective outcomes. Because both C-arms can be locked into position in advance, the operator is freed from the need to repeatedly reposition the imaging equipment during the procedure. This enhancement significantly improves procedural efficiency, reduces interruptions, and supports a more consistent and reliable imaging environment.

# Bi-Planar Fluoroscopy Systems for Enhanced Spinal Interventions

## Overview

Bi-planar fluoroscopy systems represent a significant advancement in imaging technology for surgical and interventional procedures. These systems employ dual fluoroscopes, each mounted to its own C-arm, to simultaneously capture two distinct imaging planes of a target anatomical region. Specifically, one fluoroscope is positioned to capture a lateral (side) view, while the second captures an anterior-posterior (front-to-back) view. Together, these complementary perspectives provide the operator with comprehensive spatial awareness of the target site.

## System Configuration

A defining feature of these systems is that each fluoroscope is fixed in position once the initial setup is complete. Rather than requiring the repeated manual adjustment and repositioning of a single imaging unit, both fluoroscopes remain stationary throughout the procedure. Each unit can be operated independently, allowing the operator to activate either the lateral or anterior-posterior view—or both—as needed during the intervention.

To facilitate hands-free operation, the fluoroscopes are controlled through proximal control mechanisms. These may include foot pedals that allow the operator to trigger imaging while maintaining full use of their hands, or voice command systems that respond to spoken instructions. Because these controls are accessible to a single operator, the system reduces the need for additional personnel to manage the imaging equipment, streamlining the surgical workflow.

## Clinical Advantages

The primary benefit of this configuration is the elimination of equipment repositioning after the initial setup. In conventional single-fluoroscope arrangements, capturing multiple views requires physically moving the imaging unit between positions—a process that is time-consuming, introduces potential for misalignment, and interrupts the flow of the procedure. By contrast, the bi-planar approach maintains both imaging planes continuously available, allowing the operator to switch instantly between views.

This translates into significantly enhanced procedural efficiency and reduced overall procedure time. These benefits are particularly valuable in spinal interventions, where precise instrument placement is critical. For example, during pedicle screw placement, the surgeon must accurately guide screws into the vertebral pedicles while avoiding surrounding neural and vascular structures. Similarly, in kyphoplasty procedures, the correct positioning of a balloon within a compressed vertebral body is essential for effective treatment. In both cases, the ability to rapidly confirm instrument position from two perspectives without pausing to reposition equipment improves accuracy, safety, and operative speed.

## Conclusion

By combining fixed dual-fluoroscope imaging with intuitive, hands-free control mechanisms operable by a single individual, bi-planar fluoroscopy systems offer a practical and efficient solution for complex spinal procedures. The elimination of repetitive equipment adjustment not only shortens procedure times but also enhances the consistency and reliability of intraoperative imaging, ultimately supporting improved patient outcomes.

# The and This: The Small Words That Do Big Work

Some of the most important words in the English language are also among the shortest and most overlooked. "The" and "this" are perfect examples—tiny words that we use constantly without ever stopping to appreciate how much they accomplish.

## The Power of "The"

"The" is the single most common word in the English language. It appears in nearly every sentence we speak or write, yet most of us never think about what it actually does. As the definite article, "the" tells us that we are talking about something specific and identifiable.

Consider the difference between "I saw a dog" and "I saw the dog." The first suggests any dog, unknown and undefined. The second points to a particular dog—one that both the speaker and listener already have in mind. This small word carries the weight of shared knowledge and context.

## The Function of "This"

"This" belongs to a special group of words called demonstratives. Its job is to point—to draw attention to something close by, either physically or conceptually. When you say "this book" or "this idea," you are directing focus toward something present, immediate, and near.

"This" also creates a sense of connection. It brings the subject closer to both the speaker and the reader, making the conversation feel personal and grounded in the here and now.

## Why These Words Matter

Though "the" and "this" seem simple, they reveal something profound about language: meaning often depends not on grand vocabulary, but on the quiet machinery of everyday words. These small words provide structure, clarity, and precision, helping us navigate the difference between the general and the specific, the distant and the near.

The next time you write a sentence, take a moment to notice these humble helpers. This attention to the smallest words can transform ordinary writing into something clear and intentional.

# Bi-Planar Fluoroscopy System for Spinal Procedures

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

### Field of the Invention

The present invention relates generally to medical imaging systems, and more particularly to a bi-planar fluoroscopy system employing dual fluoroscopic imaging assemblies mounted on separate C-arm structures to provide simultaneous lateral and anteroposterior (AP) imaging during spinal surgical procedures and interventional treatments.

### Description of the Related Art

Fluoroscopic imaging has become an indispensable tool in modern spinal surgery, interventional pain management, and minimally invasive spinal procedures. Fluoroscopy enables surgeons to visualize anatomical structures, surgical instruments, and implantable devices in real time, thereby facilitating accurate placement of pedicle screws, needles, catheters, and other surgical hardware while minimizing tissue disruption.

Conventional fluoroscopic systems typically employ a single C-arm apparatus comprising an X-ray source and an opposing image detector or intensifier. During a typical spinal procedure, the surgeon or radiologic technologist must repeatedly reposition the single C-arm to alternate between lateral views and anteroposterior views of the surgical site. This repositioning is necessary because accurate three-dimensional placement of spinal instrumentation generally requires visualization from at least two substantially orthogonal planes.

The reliance on a single C-arm presents several significant disadvantages. First, the repeated repositioning of the imaging apparatus between the lateral and AP orientations consumes considerable procedural time, prolonging both the duration of surgery and the associated anesthesia exposure for the patient. Second, each repositioning introduces the potential for registration errors, as the anatomical reference points may shift relative to the imaging device between successive views. Third, the surgeon frequently must interrupt the surgical workflow, cease active manipulation of instruments, and wait for the imaging apparatus to be repositioned before confirming trajectory or depth in a second plane.

Perhaps most critically, the cumulative radiation exposure associated with repeated single-plane imaging poses substantial risks to patients and to operating room personnel. Because each transition between planes typically requires acquisition of new images to reestablish the anatomical view, the total fluoroscopic exposure time is substantially increased relative to what would be required if both planes could be visualized concurrently.

Attempts to address these limitations have included the use of biplane angiographic suites; however, such systems are generally fixed, ceiling-mounted or floor-mounted installations designed primarily for cardiovascular and neurovascular applications. These fixed systems are prohibitively expensive, occupy dedicated procedure rooms, lack the mobility required for general surgical use, and are not readily adaptable to the diverse patient positioning requirements encountered in spinal surgery. Moreover, fixed biplane systems often present physical obstructions that impede surgeon access to the operative field and complicate the sterile draping of the patient.

There remains a need in the art for a fluoroscopy system that provides simultaneous multi-planar imaging capability, that retains the mobility and flexibility associated with conventional C-arm apparatus, that reduces cumulative radiation exposure, and that streamlines surgical workflow during spinal procedures.

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present invention overcomes the aforementioned limitations of the prior art by providing a bi-planar fluoroscopy system comprising two independently positionable C-arm fluoroscopic assemblies configured to simultaneously acquire lateral and anteroposterior images of a spinal surgical site.

In accordance with one aspect of the invention, the system comprises a first C-arm fluoroscope assembly having a first X-ray source and a first opposing image detector, the first assembly being oriented to acquire a lateral image of a patient's spine. The system further comprises a second C-arm fluoroscope assembly having a second X-ray source and a second opposing image detector, the second assembly being oriented substantially orthogonally to the first assembly to acquire an anteroposterior image of the patient's spine. The two C-arm assemblies are arranged such that their respective imaging planes intersect at a common region of interest corresponding to the surgical site.

In accordance with another aspect of the invention, the system includes a control subsystem operatively coupled to both the first and second C-arm assemblies. The control subsystem coordinates the operation of the two X-ray sources so as to reduce or eliminate cross-scatter interference between the two imaging channels. In certain embodiments, the control subsystem employs temporal multiplexing, whereby the two X-ray sources are pulsed in alternating, interleaved fashion at a frequency sufficient to present the operator with the perception of two continuous, simultaneous image streams while preventing radiation emitted by one source from being received by the detector associated with the other source.

In accordance with a further aspect of the invention, the system includes a display subsystem configured to present the lateral image and the anteroposterior image concurrently, either on separate display monitors or in a side-by-side or picture-in-picture arrangement on a common display. This concurrent display enables the surgeon to continuously monitor instrument trajectory and depth in two orthogonal planes without interrupting the surgical workflow.

In accordance with yet another aspect of the invention, each C-arm assembly is independently mobile and positionable, retaining the flexibility and accessibility advantages of conventional single C-arm systems while providing the multi-planar imaging benefits heretofore available only from fixed biplane installations. In some embodiments, the two C-arm assemblies are provided with a registration subsystem that spatially correlates the two imaging planes, enabling the derivation of three-dimensional positional information regarding surgical instruments and anatomical structures from the two two-dimensional image streams.

The bi-planar fluoroscopy system of the present invention offers numerous advantages over the prior art, including: substantially reduced procedural time by eliminating the need to reposition a single C-arm between planes; reduced cumulative radiation exposure to the patient and operating room personnel; improved accuracy in the placement of spinal instrumentation through continuous orthogonal visualization; enhanced surgical workflow continuity; and retention of the mobility and cost-effectiveness associated with C-arm based systems.

These and other features, aspects, and advantages of the present invention will become better understood with reference to the following description, appended claims, and accompanying drawings.

---

*Note: This is a sample drafting for illustrative purposes. Actual patent applications should be prepared or reviewed by a registered patent attorney or agent, and a thorough prior art search should be conducted to ensure novelty and non-obviousness before filing.*

# Dual-Fluoroscope Imaging System for Pedicle Screw Placement

## Invention Overview

A biplanar fluoroscopic imaging system employing two fixed C-arms positioned orthogonally (AP and lateral simultaneously), enabling real-time cross-referenced visualization during spinal instrumentation—controlled by a single operator through a unified interface.

## Core Components

**1. Dual Fixed C-Arm Configuration**
- Two C-arms mounted on ceiling/floor rails positioned at ~90° to each other
- One provides continuous **anteroposterior (AP)** view; the other provides **lateral** view
- Fixed geometry eliminates need for repeated repositioning during a procedure

**2. Unified Control Console**
- Single foot pedal array with distinct pedals for: AP-only, lateral-only, or simultaneous dual-plane acquisition
- Touchscreen/voice interface allowing hands-free image capture while maintaining sterile field
- Ergonomic layout so the surgeon controls imaging without a dedicated radiology technologist

**3. Synchronized Pulse Timing**
- Alternating pulsed emission between the two X-ray sources prevents **cross-scatter interference** (one detector receiving stray photons from the opposite emitter)
- Interleaved firing at high frequency creates the perception of simultaneous dual-view imaging

## Key Innovations for Screw Placement

**4. Cross-Referenced Trajectory Display**
- Software overlays a virtual pedicle screw trajectory on both views simultaneously
- Adjusting the tool in one plane updates the projected position in the orthogonal plane in real time
- Displays entry point, angle, and predicted depth against vertebral anatomy

**5. Instrument Tracking Integration**
- Optical or electromagnetic tracking correlates the physical awl/tap/screw driver with both fluoroscopic planes
- Warns of medial/lateral pedicle wall breach before it occurs

## Benefits

| Feature | Clinical Advantage |
|---------|-------------------|
| Simultaneous biplanar view | Eliminates C-arm rotation between AP/lateral checks |
| Single-operator control | Reduces staffing and communication errors |
| Reduced fluoroscopy time | Lower radiation dose to patient and staff |
| Real-time trajectory feedback | Improved screw accuracy, fewer breaches |

## Radiation Safety
- Pulsed, alternating acquisition minimizes cumulative dose
- Automatic collimation to region of interest
- Dose-tracking dashboard displayed on console

---

# Technical Summary: Dual-Fluoroscope Imaging System for Kyphoplasty

## System Overview

This medical imaging system employs two fluoroscopic C-arm units fixed in orthogonal orientations to provide simultaneous biplanar visualization during percutaneous kyphoplasty procedures. By eliminating the need to reposition a single C-arm between projections, the system reduces procedure time, minimizes radiation exposure through optimized imaging workflows, and enhances surgical precision during vertebral augmentation.

## Configuration

**Fluoroscope Positioning**
- **AP (Anteroposterior) Unit:** Locked in a vertical orientation to capture coronal-plane imaging of the target vertebral body, pedicle alignment, and instrument trajectory.
- **Lateral Unit:** Fixed in a horizontal orientation perpendicular to the AP unit, providing sagittal-plane visualization for depth assessment, needle advancement, and cement deposition monitoring.

The orthogonal locked configuration maintains consistent registration between the two planes, allowing the surgeon to interpret three-dimensional anatomy from stable, reproducible reference frames throughout the procedure.

## Control Interfaces

**Foot Pedal Control**
- Dedicated pedals allow hands-free activation of each fluoroscope independently or simultaneously.
- Maintains sterile field integrity while keeping the operator's hands engaged with surgical instruments.
- Configurable pedal mapping for AP-only, lateral-only, or biplanar exposure modes.

**Voice Command Control**
- Speech recognition interface enables activation of imaging sequences, magnification adjustments, image capture, and last-image-hold functions.
- Reduces dependence on circulating staff for imaging adjustments.
- Command set optimized for a low-noise recognition environment with confirmation feedback to prevent inadvertent exposures.

## Clinical Workflow Benefits

| Feature | Benefit |
|---------|---------|
| Biplanar simultaneous imaging | Eliminates C-arm repositioning between AP and lateral views |
| Hands-free control | Preserves sterility and surgical continuity |
| Locked orthogonal geometry | Ensures consistent, reproducible imaging planes |
| Real-time dual visualization | Improves accuracy of trocar placement and cement injection |
| Reduced staff intervention | Streamlines workflow and shortens procedure duration |

## Radiation Safety Considerations

- **Pulsed fluoroscopy modes** minimize cumulative dose during continuous monitoring phases such as cement injection.
- **Last-image-hold (LIH)** functionality reduces unnecessary live exposure.
- Independent activation permits selective imaging, avoiding redundant biplanar exposure when only one view is required.
- Dose reporting and tracking for both units support ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) compliance.

## Kyphoplasty-Specific Applications

During kyphoplasty, the system supports critical procedural steps:
1. **Trocar Insertion:** Biplanar guidance confirms transpedicular trajectory and prevents medial or inferior cortical breach.
2. **Balloon Tamp Placement and Inflation:** Real-time dual-plane monitoring of void creation and vertebral height restoration.
3. **Cement (PMMA) Delivery:** Continuous lateral visualization detects extravasation into the spinal canal or vascular structures, while AP imaging confirms symmetric fill.

## Summary

By integrating two locked-position fluoroscopes with hands-free foot pedal and voice command control, this system addresses the primary inefficiencies of conventional single C-arm kyphoplasty—repeated repositioning, workflow interruption, and prolonged exposure. The result is a more efficient, ergonomic, and precise imaging platform that supports enhanced procedural safety and reduced operative time.

---

*Note: This is a conceptual technical summary. Actual system deployment requires validation against regulatory standards (FDA/CE), institutional radiation safety protocols, and clinical verification.*

counterfactuals.output:
# Bi-planar Fluoroscopy in Spinal Surgery

## The Core Problem with Single-Plane Imaging

In conventional single C-arm fluoroscopy, surgeons need to visualize anatomy from **two perpendicular views** to safely place hardware (like pedicle screws):

- **Anteroposterior (AP)** view — shows medial/lateral positioning
- **Lateral view** — shows cranial/caudal trajectory and depth

With a single C-arm, obtaining both views requires **physically rotating or repositioning** the equipment between shots, which introduces several time costs.

## How Bi-planar Setup Eliminates Repositioning

A bi-planar system uses **two separate imaging chains** (two source-detector pairs) oriented orthogonally, providing simultaneous AP and lateral imaging.

| Step | Single C-arm | Bi-planar |
|------|-------------|-----------|
| Get AP view | Position C-arm | Already available |
| Switch to lateral | **Rotate ~90°** | Already available |
| Re-confirm AP | **Rotate back** | Already available |
| Verify final position | Multiple rotations | Instant dual-view |

## Specific Time Savings

**1. No mechanical rotation delays**
Each C-arm rotation takes time to move, stabilize, and avoid collisions with the patient, table, and sterile field.

**2. Elimination of re-registration**
After moving a C-arm, the surgeon must often re-establish orientation and reconfirm the target level, repeating alignment steps.

**3. Reduced instrument "pausing"**
Surgeons can advance instruments under **continuous dual-view guidance** rather than stopping to reimage in a new plane.

**4. Fewer redundant exposures**
Instead of shooting AP → move → lateral → move → re-verify, both planes update in real time as hardware advances.

**5. Preserved sterile workflow**
No need to break rhythm to have staff reposition equipment around the draped field.

## Secondary Benefits

- **Lower radiation** (fewer repeated shots to re-find views)
- **Improved accuracy** through real-time cross-referencing
- **Less staff coordination** for equipment movement

---

Would you like me to go deeper on any aspect — such as the radiation dose tradeoffs, specific applications like kyphoplasty vs. pedicle screw placement, or how this compares to 3D navigation systems?

# Summary of the Invention

The present invention provides methods and systems for simultaneous lateral and anterior-posterior fluoroscopic imaging using two independently controlled fluoroscopes. The invention addresses long-standing limitations in conventional single-plane and biplane fluoroscopy by enabling coordinated yet independent control of multiple imaging systems, thereby providing clinicians with real-time, multi-perspective visualization during interventional procedures while reducing radiation exposure and improving workflow efficiency.

## Overview

In one aspect, the present invention provides a system comprising a first fluoroscope configured to acquire image data along a lateral imaging axis and a second fluoroscope configured to acquire image data along an anterior-posterior imaging axis. The first and second fluoroscopes are independently controllable with respect to one or more operational parameters, including but not limited to positioning, angulation, source-to-image distance, radiation dose, pulse rate, collimation, and image acquisition timing. A control system operatively coupled to both fluoroscopes coordinates their operation to enable substantially simultaneous acquisition of lateral and anterior-posterior images of a target anatomy.

## Coordinated Independent Control

In certain embodiments, the control system includes a synchronization module that governs the temporal relationship between image acquisitions from the first and second fluoroscopes. The synchronization module may operate the fluoroscopes in a truly simultaneous mode, in which both fluoroscopes emit radiation and acquire images concurrently, or in an interleaved mode, in which the fluoroscopes alternate radiation emission to minimize cross-scatter interference between the two imaging planes. In the interleaved mode, the temporal offset between acquisitions may be sufficiently small that the resulting images are perceived by an operator as effectively simultaneous.

In a further aspect, the independent controllability of each fluoroscope permits the operational parameters of the first fluoroscope to be adjusted without necessitating corresponding adjustment of the second fluoroscope. For example, radiation dose, frame rate, or collimation for the lateral view may be optimized independently of the anterior-posterior view, allowing each imaging plane to be tailored to the specific anatomical structures and clinical requirements associated with that projection.

## Scatter Mitigation

In some embodiments, the system incorporates one or more scatter mitigation features to reduce degradation of image quality resulting from radiation scatter between the two imaging planes. Such features may include temporal interleaving of radiation pulses as described above, spatial or spectral filtering, anti-scatter grids, and computational scatter-correction algorithms applied to the acquired image data. In particular embodiments, the control system dynamically coordinates the pulse timing of the first and second fluoroscopes such that radiation emission from one fluoroscope does not substantially overlap with the image detection window of the other fluoroscope.

## Image Processing and Display

In another aspect, the invention provides for the processing and display of the acquired lateral and anterior-posterior images. The system may include a display subsystem configured to present the lateral and anterior-posterior images concurrently, either on separate display regions or in a combined visualization. In certain embodiments, image data from the two fluoroscopes is registered to a common coordinate system, enabling reconstruction of three-dimensional spatial information regarding a device, instrument, or anatomical structure within the imaging field. This capability facilitates accurate localization and navigation during interventional procedures.

## Registration and Spatial Correlation

In further embodiments, the control system maintains a known geometric relationship between the first and second fluoroscopes, whether through fixed mechanical calibration, real-time position tracking, or a combination thereof. The known geometric relationship enables spatial correlation of features appearing in the lateral and anterior-posterior images. In embodiments employing position tracking, the system may include sensors or encoders that report the position and orientation of each fluoroscope to the control system, permitting recalibration of the spatial relationship following independent repositioning of either fluoroscope.

## Advantages

Embodiments of the present invention provide numerous advantages over conventional fluoroscopic imaging systems. By enabling simultaneous acquisition of lateral and anterior-posterior views using independently controlled fluoroscopes, the invention eliminates the need to reposition a single fluoroscope between projections, thereby reducing procedure time and improving continuity of visualization. The independent controllability of each fluoroscope permits optimization of imaging parameters for each projection, improving image quality while managing overall radiation dose. The scatter mitigation features preserve image quality despite the presence of two concurrently operating imaging systems. Collectively, these features enhance the safety, efficiency, and effectiveness of interventional and diagnostic procedures.

## Scope

It is to be understood that the foregoing summary describes certain aspects and embodiments of the invention and is not intended to limit the scope of the invention as defined by the claims. Various features described herein may be combined in any suitable manner, and additional features, aspects, and advantages of the invention will be apparent from the following detailed description, drawings, and claims.
